newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl confident euro coming despite doubts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl confident euro coming despite doubts.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday he was confident the single European currency would be launched on schedule in 1999 even though comments by German and French officials have raised new doubts about the euro's chances.

Reporting to parliament on the European Union and Group of Seven summits, Kohl said economic and monetary union (EMU) was vital because it would stimulate growth and secure jobs. He warned of dark consequences if EMU were delayed or scrapped.

"To abandon EMU would mean Europe was giving up on its great challenge at a decisive moment," Kohl said. "That would bring all the negative consequences for exports, investment and jobs in Germany and harm Europe's integration. We would all pay dearly for the failure of the euro."

But several threads in the euro project appeared to unravel when France said it would not meet the required deficit criteria standards this year and a leading German euro-sceptic, Bavarian premier and Kohl political ally Edmund Stoiber, poured more cold water on the project.

Adding to the ominous mood, Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said Germany would have a hard time qualifying for the EMU stability criteria and warned there could be a "disaster of disintegration" in Europe if the new currency were weak.
"There is a sober verdict steadily gaining ground that France is unwilling and Germany unable... to satisfy the criteria," Jochimsen said in a speech in Bonn.

"It does not take much imagination to conclude that states which fail to observe the criteria now will fail to do so in future," said Jochimsen, who is also central bank president in the opposition Social Democrat-ruled state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday night the country's deficit would not be cut to the EMU target 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.

Because it is widely believed that monetary union cannot begin without Germany and France as members, Strauss-Kahn's statement could fuel speculation that monetary union will begin even if members have not achieved the 3.0 percent goal. The goal is among the targets of the Maastricht Treaty for monetary union and Germany has in the past insisted on strict adherance to the targets to ensure a strong start for the euro.

The prospect of a soft euro has angered Stoiber, who, like Kohl, is a conservative. Stoiber has consistently played to voter fears of giving up their deutschemark. Public opinion polls regularly show a majority of Germans opposed to trading in their marks for the proposed euro.

The mass daily Bild newspaper on Friday said Stoiber had decided he would vote against the introduction of the euro in Germany's upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, if all the Maastricht criteria were not met.
"This is not a debate about decimal points (above 3.0 percent) but rather a question of trust in a stable euro for the financial markets and public." Stoiber said.
Kohl, who at times sounded uncharacteristically defensive in his speech to parliament, said the treaty agreed at the EU summit in Amsrerdam had advanced integration on several fronts.
Sounding as if he were trying to convince doubters, Kohl repeated the line "the euro is coming" on four occasions.

The chancellor said the "clear signal" from Amsterdam was that the euro was now inevitable and that his party was unified on that point, a remark that drew derisive laughter from the opposition benches.
Opposition leaders pointed to the row between Kohl and Stoiber as evidence the chancellor was losing his grip on the ruling centre-right coalition.
"I am certain that we will introduce the euro according to plan -- punctually on January 1, 1999 and fully in line with the Maastricht criteria," Kohl said.
"There will be no tampering with the schedule and criteria," he said. "The euro is coming -- as a stable currency and a sound foundation for a bright economic future for Europe."

Kohl said euro would also secure peace and freedom in Europe. "If we want Europe and especially Germany to succeed in free market competition then we must act responsibly and ensure that the euro is implemented."
